text: As the audience thinned, the chase led us at last into the most noisome quarter of London, where everything bore the worst impress of deplorable poverty and of desperate crime. <break time="0.8s" /> Here the old man brightened up like a lamp nearly burnt out that suddenly flares again, and he strode once more with an elastic step among the wretched figures still roaming the lanes. <break time="0.8s" /> Near daybreak we reached one of the huge suburban temples of Intemperance, and with a half shriek of joy the old man forced his way in, resuming at once his aimless pacing among the throng. <break time="0.8s" /> Before long, however, a rush to the door showed that the host was closing up for the night, and the look upon the old mans face at that moment was more intense than despair itself. <break time="0.8s" /> Yet he did not hesitate in his career, but with a mad energy retraced his steps at once to the heart of mighty London, where all day long he wandered to and fro amid the turmoil. <break time="0.8s" /> As the shades of the second evening came on, I grew wearied unto death, and stopping fully in front of the wanderer, I gazed at him steadfastly in the face, yet he did not notice me. <break time="0.8s" /> This old man, I said at length, is the type and the genius of deep crime, he refuses to be alone, and he is the man of the crowd. <break time="0.8s" /> It will be in vain to follow, for I shall learn no more of him, and perhaps it is but one of the great mercies of God that the worst heart of the world does not permit itself to be read.
